idiom_name: state objects as structs of function pointers (hand-written vtable)
implementation_notes: C has neither inheritance nor dynamic dispatch, so the State/ConcreteState hierarchy is hand-written: a struct of function pointers (an explicit vtable) per state and a context struct that points at the current state object; handlers take the context as their first parameter and transition by assigning ctx->state = &next_state. States without data are file-scope static const instances, which gives the shared-stateless-states consequence for free, while anything per-context belongs in the context struct. A table of (state, event) -> handler entries is the C analogue of a transition table and keeps the graph inspectable; there is no classic form to replace here, the manual structure is the pattern.
pitfalls: A handler that forgets to assign ctx->state silently stays in its state; nothing checks that every (state, event) pair is covered.
Function-pointer tables are shared constant data: putting per-context fields in a static State makes two contexts corrupt each other.
Calling through a mismatched function-pointer type needs a cast, compiles, and fails at runtime; keep one typedef per handler signature and cast only where the pointer is stored.
